They know how clever the boy is; he'll get life. They won't give the Artful anything short of life.”

“What d'you mean by lagging and a lifer?” Mr. Bolter demanded. “What's the use of talking like that to me? Why can't you speak so I know what you're saying?”

Fagin was on the point of rendering these obscure expressions into ordinary speech. Had he done so, Mr. Bolter would have learned that they meant “transportation for life.” But their conversation was interrupted by Master Bates, who entered with both hands in his breeches pockets and a face drawn into a half-comical expression of grief.

“It's all over, Fagin,” Charley announced, once introductions to his new companion had been made.

“What do you mean?”

“They've got the gentleman whose box it is, and two or three more are coming to identify him. The Artful's booked to sail,” answered Master Bates. “I must have a whole mourning suit, Fagin, with a hatband, to visit him before he goes traveling. Think of Jack Dawkins—splendid Jack—the Dodger—the Artful Dodger—being sent overseas for an ordinary tuppenny-ha'penny snuffbox! I'd never have expected him to manage it for less than a gold watch, chain, and seals, at the very least. Oh, why couldn't he have stripped some rich old gentleman of every valuable he possessed, and gone out like a gentleman, instead of a common thief with no honor or glory?”

Having thus expressed his concern for his unfortunate friend, Master Bates sank into the nearest chair, looking dejected and mortified.

“What do you mean, saying he has no honor or glory?” Fagin cried, casting an angry glance at his pupil. “Wasn't he always the best of the lot of you? Could any one of you equal him, or get anywhere near him on any job? Eh?”

“Not one,” Master Bates answered, his voice thick with sorrow. “Not a single one.”

“Then what are you talking about?” Fagin retorted angrily. “What's all this crying for?”

“Because it isn't in the record, is it?” said Charley, his flood of regret driving him into outright defiance of his venerable friend. “Because it can't appear in the indictment. Because nobody will ever know half of what he was. What sort of entry will he get in the Newgate Calendar? Maybe none at all. Oh, my eye, my eye, what a blow!”

“Ha! Ha!” Fagin cried, stretching out his right hand and turning to Mr. Bolter. His fit of chuckling shook him as though he suffered from palsy. “Look at the pride they have in their profession, my dear.

“I must leave without knowing my fate; but I shall come back here, or seek out your party, as soon as I can. A glance, a single word, will settle whether I enter your father's house tonight or never again.”

A letter of this kind could not quickly be recovered from. Thirty minutes alone with her thoughts might have restored her composure. The mere ten minutes before she was disturbed, constrained as she was by her circumstances, could bring her no such calm. Each passing moment seemed instead to deepen her agitation. Her happiness was overwhelming. Before she had emerged from its first flood of feeling, Charles, Mary, and Henrietta arrived together.

The urgent necessity of appearing her usual self made her struggle at once; after a little time, however, she could maintain the effort no longer. Their words ceased to make any sense to her, and she had to excuse herself by pleading illness. Now they noticed how unwell she looked. Alarmed and anxious, they would not dream of leaving without her. This was intolerable. If only they had gone away and let her enjoy the room in peace, she would have needed no other remedy. Having them all waiting or standing about her was unbearable, and in desperation she announced that she would go home.

“Certainly, my dear,” Mrs Musgrove exclaimed. “Go home at once and look after yourself, so that you'll be well enough for tonight. I wish Sarah were here to treat you, but I'm no doctor. Charles, ring for a chair. She mustn't walk.”

A chair, however, was out of the question: worse than anything! To forfeit the chance of exchanging a few words with Captain Wentworth during a quiet, solitary walk up through the town was unthinkable; she felt almost certain she would meet him. She protested earnestly against the chair. Mrs Musgrove, whose thoughts admitted only one kind of illness, anxiously established that there had been no fall: Anne had not recently slipped and struck her head; she was entirely sure that she had suffered no fall at all. Once reassured, Mrs Musgrove could let her leave contentedly, confident of finding her better that evening.

Determined to neglect no possible precaution, Anne made an effort and said,

“I'm afraid, ma'am, that our meaning may not be quite clear. Please be so kind as to tell the other gentlemen that we hope to welcome your entire party this evening. I fear there has been some misunderstanding, and I particularly wish you to assure Captain Harville and Captain Wentworth that we hope to see them both.”

“Oh, my dear, they understand it perfectly, I promise you.

When Tom woke that morning, he could not think where he was. He sat up, rubbed his eyes, and glanced around. Then he remembered. Dawn was cool and gray, and the deep quiet of the woods gave him a wonderful feeling of rest and peace. No leaf moved; no sound disturbed nature's thoughts. Drops of dew stood like beads on the grass and leaves. White ash covered the fire, and a thin blue wisp of smoke rose straight upward. Joe and Huck were still asleep.

A bird called somewhere far off among the trees. Another answered, and soon a woodpecker began tapping. Slowly the cool gray light grew pale, while sounds increased and living things began to stir. The thoughtful boy watched the wonder of nature waking and beginning its day's work. A small green worm crawled across a wet leaf. Now and then it raised two-thirds of its body into the air and “sniffed around” before moving on. It was measuring, Tom decided. When it turned toward him of its own accord, he stayed perfectly still. His hopes rose whenever it continued in his direction and sank whenever it seemed likely to turn aside. At last it paused for an agonizing moment with its body curved in the air, then lowered itself firmly onto Tom's leg and set off across him. His heart filled with delight. That meant he would get a new suit of clothes, and surely it would be a splendidly showy pirate's uniform. A line of ants appeared from nowhere in particular and began their work. One struggled bravely past, carrying a dead spider five times its own size, and hauled the burden straight up a tree trunk. A spotted brown ladybug climbed to the dizzying top of a blade of grass. Tom leaned close and said, “Ladybug, ladybug, fly away home, your house is on fire, your children are alone.” She opened her wings and flew away to investigate. This did not surprise him. He had long known how readily this insect believed reports of fire and had fooled it more than once before. Next came a dung beetle, pushing hard against its ball. Tom touched it so he could watch it fold its legs against its body and pretend to be dead. By now the birds were making a tremendous commotion. A catbird, the northern mimic, landed in a tree above his head and joyfully sang imitations of the other birds. Then a shrieking jay flashed down like a blue flame and settled on a twig almost within reach. It tilted its head and studied the strangers with intense curiosity. A gray squirrel and a large fox squirrel scurried past, stopping now and then to sit upright, examine the boys, and chatter at them. These wild creatures had probably never seen a human before and could scarcely decide whether they should be afraid.
